author: winter oak
title: The island that broke free
content:
A book review by Paul Cudenec, who reads it 

here




“Every word that comes from your speaking hole is a lie in some form”. [1]




“You, the self-designated Elite of this planet, brought to your position moreso by your own lack of what is understood in most places as morality and your willingness over millennia to steal and cheat and perform the most barbaric crimes… have betrayed your trust about as fully as any trust could be betrayed”. [2]




Dave Patterson does not mince his words in 

Greenways

 – the first of two “

Green Island

” books – which although a work of fiction features a large amount of truth.




The basis of the novel is that Prince Edward Island in eastern Canada has partly broken away from the rest of the country after a surprise election result that ended the old two-party hold on power.




It has renamed itself Green Island and started organising society in a very different way to the previous status quo.




Now, the description of a stable and mainly happy society (not quite a Utopia, but heading that way) could have been as dull as ditchwater over the nearly 600 pages of Patterson’s work.










But he does a great job in making the book a lively read. For a start, his style (or styles, because he adopts many different registers according to who is speaking or writing) is one of anything but terse concision – ebullient eloquence would be nearer the mark and there is plenty of humour as well.




Neither is Patterson of the social realist school, as evidenced by the way that the island attracts the interest and presence of 

Henry David Thoreau

, [3] Thomas More, Thomas Paine and Che Guevera and that the trial of the global elite featured in the opening citations is conducted by a divine presence called The One, accompanied by the blindfolded figure of Justice herself.




There are several distinct threads advancing through the pages, including chapters consisting of fragments and thought-provoking quotations from famous thinkers.




I will share a few of the latter to give you a flavour:







“Do not go where the path may lead; go instead where there is no path and leave a trail”. Ralph Waldo Emerson. [4]










“Whatever you do will seem insignificant, but it is very important to do it”. 

Mohandas Gandhi

. [5]










“Justice is conscience, not a personal conscience but the conscience of the whole of humanity. Those who clearly recognize the voice of their own conscience usually recognize also the voice of justice”. Alexander Solzhenitsyn. [6]










“The trade of governing has always been monopolised by the most ignorant and the most rascally individuals of mankind”. Thomas Paine. [7]










“When plunder becomes a way of life for a group of men living in society, they create for themselves, in the course of time, a legal system that authorizes it and a moral code that glorifies it”. Frédéric Bastiat. [8]













But there is also plenty of wisdom in 

Greenways

 to be found coming from the mouths, pens and keyboards of its various characters, all of which can of course be regarded as 

Dave Patterson

 quotations. Here are some of them:







“Strength guided by a reptilian mind is not conducive to advanced civilization”. [9]










“At all times the power of a tiny point of Light is such that it will dissipate darkness all around, but the power of a tiny point of darkness in a place where there is Light is insignificant”. [10]










“I remember still when we had plenty and freedom in our village here, and happiness and security and a good life in our families, and no ruler… It was a simpler life, to be sure, but one I know most would joyfully return to, rather than what we have now”. [11]










“After a certain period of training, the people embrace their chains, they love their chains, they hate those who try to free them!” [12]







That last one reminds me of the multiple occasions when I would be using a day off work (Saturdays, usually) to make a stand for freedom, only for some chain-loving passer-by to angrily call out: “

Getta job!

“.










Only five years into their new era, the islanders’ world is still not too different from our own, although they are proud to be “turning back some of the less pleasant aspects of modern industrial society”. [13]




Traffic has been reduced because of “a good reliable public transport system” [14] and they enjoy permaculture and organic market gardens. [15]




Since Green Island is a real democracy I find myself hoping that they will reverse themselves yet further out of the industrial dead-end and collectively decide that their airport, solar panels and wind turbines are not compatible with the restoration of natural harmony.




They are making a healthy start, anyway: “The people are coming from the cocoons and boxes in droves, turning off the sedating tvs and abandoning the meds and malls to finally start living lives of optimism and trust and honesty that come naturally to most people”. [16]




“It’s really quite amazing the amount of energy and ideas out there, that have been stifled for so long. We’re really like a wonderful flower – or strong tree, perhaps! – whose seed has been buried somewhere and not allowed to germinate, and now with the sunlight springing up almost overnight, joyously full of life”. [17]




“We’ve let the people out of a dark dungeon into the true light for the first time in their lives, and there is no way they are going back”. [18]










There is a strong sense of social justice in the imagined breakaway society, which Patterson uses to expose the lack of it in the world we inhabit.




“On Green Island, for instance, you will never find, anymore, a situation of a common factory employee making barely enough money in a full week of hard work to pay for the cheapest food and substandard housing, while the exalted CEO takes home a million or two dollars per week, plus a bonus of tens of millions at the end of the year and a golden parachute of hundreds of millions after a couple of years of driving the business into the ground – such things are common in Canada or the US, but really they’re signs of a severely dysfunctional system, a system based on various kinds of elitism and fraud and lies and corruption and rule by your secretive uber-elite, which we have basically managed to get rid of here, through the open we-the-people government system”. [19]




The whole point of the novel is to simultaneously condemn contemporary society and propose a sane alternative, so the author often uses the same device.




He says, for example: “The aesthetics of living pleasurably were always considered by the people who planned things on Green Island, unlike the previous systems where the efficient acquistion of money was the driving force, and little attention paid at all to making things pleasant for the people”. [20]




He has an elderly resident declare: “It’s altogether a new idea, you know, making our own decisions as a community and actually having the government do what we want rather than having them politicians sitting on the stage and telling us what they’re going to do whether or not we much approve”. [21]










And on the issue of education, he says the “old” system was “the human equivalent of dog obedience school, where children were, and still are in most places, taught primarily one thing – to go somewhere every day in the morning and do what they are told to do all day, without asking questions”. [22]




More broadly, we learn: “What we have done here, the huge accomplishment, is that we have removed (or mostly removed, there are still some lingering pockets of illness) the ‘uber-layer’ as someone called it, that great invisible sucking vacuum above us all that used to suck half of everything we did or produced straight into the bank accounts of a gang of bankers and ‘investors’ (read ‘crooks’, from my perspective) – imagine if you had some big parasite on your back, taking half your blood every day, half your food, half your energy, imagine how you’d feeel if that lump was removed, and that’s what we have done for Green Island – and it’s fabulous”. [23]




As will be apparent from the above passage, the “golden goose treadmill” [24] of the bankster class is an evil which Patterson rightly identifies as a crucially important one – “the greatest scam in all of human history”. [25]




He adds: “And the same people who own the banks, and some other wealthy ‘investors’, own the newspapers so the newspapers won’t talk about it, and they bribe the politicians so the politicians don’t talk about it”. [26]




Patterson asks: “Do you think that if the government is short of money it should allow commercial banks to create the money and then borrow it from them at prime rates of interest which you will pay for with your taxes, or that the government might better create that money itself?”. [27]










One Green Islander tells a young visitor: “Last count I saw – get a grip on something here, boy, this is a biggie – the Canadian banks had collected over a TRILLION dollars in interest on 

just

 the so-called Canadian National Debt just during the last 25 years or so, a trillion dollars of the tax money paid by your folks and every other Canadian taxpayer, a trillion dollars your folks should NOT have paid, it was really stolen”. [28]




And Patterson explains the sinister and pernicious effect of the interest attached to the money circulating in our society, which amounts to a deliberate long-term dispossession by usury.




“When banks create 98% (give or take!) of your money supply, and demand collateral and interest – well, where does the interest come from?




“They create the principal, but not the interest. Time comes to pay interest, and although all the players shuffle around the money, eventually, like a big game of musical chairs, someone cannot find interest, and collateral goes to banks.




“Every year, a lot of people cannot find interest and collateral goes to banks. Every year interest, every year collateral to banks. Over time – well, you can see where it is heading, I am sure. The slow, but ever faster, turning over of all property in your society to the banks – or, more correctly of course, the ‘investors’ who own the banks”. [29]










Finally, I was delighted to read how divine justice is meted out to a leading figure in this usurious criminal enterprise, the head of certain notorious banking dynasty by the name of Shield, who admits to having led humanity along the path “to the New World Order we have implemented today”. [30]




The One thunders angrily in the courtroom: “What would you have to say about that, Banker? About the many, nay the countless!, dreams, great and small, you have destroyed cruelly over the years, as your ancestors gathered their gold, and spread their lies, and turned the pure dreams of the people into the darkness and pain of the satanic mill in the name of this gold, into the endless slaughter of the battlefield in the pursuit of this gold, into the destruction of this endlessly beautiful planet its very self, all in the name of the pursuit of this gold?!!”. [31]




Recommended further reading: 

Enemies of the People: The Rothschilds and their corrupt global empire

. [32]

 (Green Island Book 1), (Green Island Books, 2026. Original edition 2009), p. 284,

author: winter oak
title: Feted or forgotten? A tale of two very different anarchists
content:
by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article 

here




An important split took place in the French anarchist movement at the very end of the nineteenth century.




This revolved around the question of whether the conviction of Jewish army captain Alfred Dreyfus for treason represented an important question of injustice and institutional anti-semitism or whether, 

au contraire

, the case was irrelevant to the anarchist struggle.




François Jarrige writes in the 

latest issue

 of 

Brasero: revue de contre-histoire

: “The Dreyfus affair, which tore France apart from 1897-1898 onwards, also divided the anarchist milieu”. [1]




In what he terms “an extreme polarisation”, anarchists, “traditionally distrustful of the army and the state, split into convinced 

dreyfusards

 and supporters of a strict indifference to what they considered an internal conflict within bourgeois institutions.




“Sébastien Faure, a major figure in the anarchist movement and co-founder of 

Le Libertaire

, nevertheless managed to drag a number of activists into the active defence of Dreyfus”. [2]




We’ll come back to Faure later, but first I want to relate what Jarrige has to say about one of the anarchists who refused to climb on board the 

dreyfusard

 bandwagon – 

Emile Gravelle (1855-1920)

.




He was the founder of a current in the French anarchist movement called 

naturien

 – there is no real English equivalent but the meaning is nature-loving or nature-based.










This, Jarrige explains, emerged in the Parisian 

quartier

 of Montmartre and was a current that was “critical of industrial society and its goods, idealising prehistorical and primitive living and calling for a return to nature”. [3]




Gravelle, an anarchist painter, illustrator, pamphleteer and activist, was one of the first to formulate such a critique of “progress” and “civilisation”, prefiguring the green anarchism that emerged towards the end of the twentieth century. [4]




An important influence on Gravelle’s understanding of the world was his five-year stay in Buenos Aires, after leaving his home town of Douai in northern France at the age of 30.




Jarrige writes: “At the time Argentina was going through a phase of expansion: political stabilisation after civil wars, the conquest of indigenous lands, the expansion of cattle-rearing on the great plains of the 

pampa

 and a massive influx of European immigrants. This context of brutal modernisation, mixing prosperity and social violence, had a deep impact on Gravelle…




“When he returned to France in 1890 he brought out a pamphlet in which he related his unpleasant experience. In this virulent text, 

La République argentine dénoncée

 (‘The Argentine Republic denounced’), he describes how he had been taken in by the embroidered tales of a ‘shipping agent in the 

rue de Dunkerque

‘, only to discover a reality of misery, exploitation and disillusionment.




“He writes about the diseases, the violence of the 

gauchos

, the insalubrity of the towns and the suffering of immigrants pushed into suicide or madness. This pamphlet, laced with bitterness, also bears witness to a political realization: Gravelle denounces the illusions of progress and the mechanisms of capitalist exploitation”. [5]










Gravelle’s years in South America shaped his understanding of modernity in another way. Through his encounters with indigenous Guarani people he discovered “man, in the midst of nature, happy as a god in the triumphant splendour of its strength and beauty”. [6]




Jarrige says this provided him with “an alternative model to the European ways of living shaped by industry, the growing consumerism and imperialism”. [7]




It fed his rejection of modern urbanisation and his aspiration to a way of life founded on simplicity, autonomy and closeness to nature – “when Gravelle returned to Paris, he was thus no longer simply an illustrator looking for work: he was the bearer of a vision of the world opposed to that of the European civilisation of his age”. [8]




In the early 1890s Gravelle set up home in Montmartre, a bohemian, artistic and anarchic enclave on a hill in Paris. At the time, it was still semi-rural and was imbibed with the spirit of resistance to the new urban order, inherited from the Paris Commune of 1871. 




Says Jarrige: “This landscape in transition, where the industrial smoke of the capital mixed with the last remains of rurality, deeply nourished Gravelle’s anarchist imagination”. [9]




“The rapid transformation of the 

quartier

 under the impact of urbanisation and property speculation reinforced in Gravelle’s mind the idea that modern civilisation destroys the natural conditions of human life. His drawings often show black plumes of factory smoke, collapsed quarries or silhouettes of old windmills.










“

La Butte

 [The Hill] became for him a laboratory where he could observe the advance of industrial modernity, but also a place for imagining alternatives. It symbolised a communalist tradition of protecting natural and public spaces threatened by power”. [10]




In 1894 Gravelle founded a four-page journal called 

L’Etat naturel

 (‘The natural state’), which ran for four issues until 1898. Jarrige explains that this periodical, largely written and illustrated by Gravelle himself, was at the heart of 

naturienisme

, contrasting natural human life with the misery of factory workers, the ugliness of the city and the artificiality of “civilisation”. [11]




When Gravelle started a 

naturien

 group in Montmartre in 1895 it was joined by penniless artists, singers and people who worked on the railways, in a bank or as a cobbler or barrel-maker.




Comments Jarrige: “This very mixed group testifies to the attractiveness of the idea of returning to nature among individuals facing material precarity, the rapid upheavals of urban society and political disillusionment”. [12]




“The 

naturiens

 organised conferences, talks and even banquets which sometimes attracted nearly a hundred people. Their influence rapidly spread beyond Montmartre: groups appeared at the Bastille, in the Latin Quarter and then outside the capital, notably in Toulon and Bordeaux.










“Although they were few in number – with undoubtedly never more than a hundred or so members – the movement built itself around intense publishing activity”. [13]




Journals such as 

Le Bulletin des Harmoniens

 (‘The Bulletin of the Harmonians’), 

La Debâcle sociale

 (‘The Social Disaster’), 

L’Idée libre

 (‘The Free Idea’), 

La Nouvelle Humanité

 (‘The New Humanity’) and 

Le Naturien

 flourished at this time.




Jarrige tells us: “The first of the four issues of the journal 

Le Naturien

 was, moreover, distributed beyond Paris, in Bordeaux, Dijon, Le Havre, Limoges, Marseilles, Montpellier, Roubaix, Saint-Nazaire, Toulon and Tours”. [14]




In its final issue, in 1898, Gravelle questioned the relevance of the insurrections and revolutions usually favoured by anarchists and the “left”.




He insisted: “You could perpetually behead kings, depose emperors and disembowel presidents of the Republic, but the situation will remain the same as long as there are mines, factories and building sites.




“As long as the artificiality that has been established over the centuries is considered as the base of our system of living, there will be exploitation of man by man, there will be despoilment and the ongoing and aggrevated degradation of nature…










“To those who talk of revolution while still wanting to hold on to superfluous Artifice, we say this: you are conserving elements of servitude, you will therefore always be slaves; you think you can seize control of material production to appropriate it for yourselves, but, in reality, this material production which constitutes the strength of your oppressors is quite safe from your covetous regard”. [15]




Gravelle concluded that as long as this industrial system of production existed, the people would never know freedom. “Material Progress is the fruit of slavery”, he insisted. [16]




Jarrige says that this viewpoint, so starkly in contrast with the industrialist Marxist outlook, had a considerable influence on the French anarchist scene, until Gravelle became marginalised around 1898.




In April of that year his girlfriend, said to have been “a fervent 

naturienne

 since the beginning” died in hospital for now-unknown reasons and Gravelle was left in a state of shocked grief. [17]




At the same time, as we have heard, the Dreyfus affair dominated the political scene and by refusing to get involved, Gravelle was cut off from many other anarchists, although he was still involved in the movement until his death in 1920.




He seems to have particularly fallen out of favour because of supposedly “anti-semitic” illustrations, such as that of a French farmer disposing of a human-like vegetable labelled “Rothschild”. [18]










Jarrige does not challenge the “anti-semitic” label, but I would question whether drawing a humorous caricature of a well-known Jewish banker is “anti-semitic” 

per se

 – the figure is certainly not meant to represent Jews 

as a whole

, or even all Jewish bankers, because the name “Rothschild” is specifically written on the forehead.




Is it not more likely that the target of Gravelle’s anger was the Rothschilds 

in particular

 – not “because they were Jewish” but because he knew full well that they were 

enemies of the people

 [19] and bore much responsibility for the industrial-imperial misery and slavery he had been witnessing and denouncing both in France and Argentina?




Going back to the split in the French anarchist movement, the leading 

dreyfusard

 

Sébastien Faure (1858-1942)

 is the subject of another article in the same issue of 

Brasero

.




There Anne Steiner explains that he founded the weekly journal 

Le Libertaire

 in 1895 and then the daily newspaper 

Le Journal du Peuple

 which led the anarchist charge in defence of Dreyfus and against anti-semtitism.




He is also rememberd for founding 

La Ruche

 (‘The Hive’), an experimental “alternative” boarding school which housed forty-odd girls and boys between the ages of six and 16.




Paying due credit to the 

Archives anarchistes

 website, [20] she digs deeper into Faure’s character with reference to the judicial files, released in 2018, which can be consulted 

there

. [21]










In brief, Faure was a disgusting paedocriminal. The records show that in 1903 he was seen approaching three girls aged eight to 12 years old, offering them a few coins for sexual favours; in 1904 he was seen kissing a 12-year-old girl on the mouth; in 1907 he was found in the company of a woman suspected of prostituting her 14-year-old daughter and so on and so forth. [22]




Having been caught molesting little girls in the street in 1917 he fled Paris – taking with him funds from his journal and printing press – but was captured in Marseilles, found guilty and sentenced to six months in jail. At this point it transpired that he had, of course, also been abusing the children at his school 

La Ruche

. [23]




A scandal also soon erupted over his links to disgraced politician Louis Malvy, whose Ministry of the Interior had, during his 1914-1917 term in office, paid subsidies to Faure’s 

La Ruche

 even though it had no legal status. [24]




Denying suggestions that Faure had been let off the hook for his child abuse for so long  because of his links to the state, the former prefect of the Paris police, Emile Laurent,  said that this was not how it had worked.




Faure’s constant paedocriminal activties could not have been proven in court, he insisted, but they allowed the police to exert a certain pressure on the anarchist, such as by ordering him to moderate the terms of his written and oral political statements. [25]










Steiner writes: “All the activists thus learned at this point that Sébastien Faure (

pictured

), child abuser and client of barely pubescent prostitutes, was controlled by the prefect of the police, who was perfectly well aware of his criminal activity. This evoked, even beyond the anarchist movement, a certain 

malaise

 and much questioning”. [26]




But Faure, remarkably, protested his innocence and claimed that he had been framed in a complicated and politically motivated state operation.




Others leapt to his defence and in 1919 backed up his story in a booklet called 

Une infamie. L’affaire Sébastien Faure

 (‘Scandal: The Sébastien Faure affair’).




Says Steiner: “This plea in favour of the old anarchist activist managed to quieten the doubts of those who had been troubled by his conviction and even more so by the evidence at his trial which depicted him as a very unsavoury individual. Until less than than two years later, there was a new affair”. [27]




In 1921 Faure and two other men in their early sixties were caught dragging two little girls, aged 11 and 12, into a flat in Paris, where they sexually abused them for four hours. Other victims were discovered and he was jailed for eight months. [28]




One might have thought that this would have led the French anarchist movement to finally denounce Faure and expel him from their midst.




But no – after his arrest 

Le Libertaire

 and the 

L’Union anarchiste

 published a communiqué in 

L’Humanité

 calling on the whole working class to show solidarity with this “upright and impeccable activist”. [29]










And when he had been jailed, 

Le Libertaire

 of June 17 1921 deplored his conviction for what they termed an “insignificant weakness” and hailed him as “the courageous friend of the working class”. [30]




Their version was again that he was the victim of a police set-up to discredit “the best revolutionary propagandist in the country”. Ignoring his long record of child abuse, they claimed a young girl had been cunningly placed in his path to frame him. [31]




While Faure denied child abuse, he rather gave the game away by dismissing anarchists who disapproved of such behaviour as “bourgeois”. [32]




Steiner relates how the paedocriminal was welcomed back into the anarchist fold after coming out of jail again and in 1925 was able to launch his 

L’Encyclopedie anarchiste

 project with a hundred collaborators who did not seem bothered about his character.




She adds, clearly somewhat outraged, that the “neo-malthusian activist” Jeanne Humbert (

pictured below

) completely misrepresented the facts about Faure in the 1949 biography she wrote about him.




For instance, she depicted the 1917 offence as having involved him touching and rubbing himself against 

women

 in the street, when it was really 

ten-year-old girls

.




“Regarding the 1921 conviction, it’s even worse, as she describes the abused little girls as ‘debauched minors’, children of a ‘precocious vicefulness'”. Humbert also insisted that Faure did nothing to shock anyone not “blinded” by conventional morality. [33]










I was interested, surprised even, to see that the profile of Faure on French 

Wikipedia

 

mentions

 that accusations of his paedocriminality were confirmed by the judicial archives made public eight years ago – and that it points readers to the 

Archives anarchistes

 site. [34]




It adds that he was a Freemason. “Sébastien Faure was initiated on June 28 1884 at the 

Vérité du Grand Orient de France

 lodge at Bordeaux… On November 3 1905, he joined the 

Le Progrès

 lodge in Paris. He resigned from Freemasonry on December 20 1917 after 33 years of involvement”. [35]




So there we have it.




Sébastien Faure, the police-controlled freemasonic paedophile who diverted anarchist energy into a struggle against “anti-semitism”, is still revered by the movement today.




Emile Gravelle, the anti-imperialist, anti-industrialist and nature-defending artist and campaigner who dared to poke fun at the industrial-imperialist Rothschilds, is today an obscure and half-forgotten figure.




It really is about time that 

real anarchists

 [36] got to their feet and made their presence known!

author: winter oak
title: Chinese communism and the usual suspects
content:
by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article 

here




The seizure of power by the communists in 1949 led to a brutal and murderous assault on Chinese life that was even worse than that experienced by Russians under the Bolsheviks.




In January 1958 Mao Zedong, the chairman of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), launched the regime’s second five-year plan, known as the Great Leap Forward.




Says

 

Wikipedia

: “The purpose of the plan was to use heavy industry to expedite the production of raw materials such as steel as a supplement to economic growth, similar to the Soviet model and the defining factor behind Mao’s Chinese Marxist policies.




“Mao spent ten months touring the country in 1958 to gain support for the Great Leap Forward and inspect the progress that had already been made. What this entailed was the humiliation, public castigation and torture of all who questioned the leap”. [1]




This rapid industrial “growth” and “development”, with people being sucked from the countryside into the cities, was a disaster – millions died from the resulting famine.




Author Frank Dikötter puts the death toll from 1958 to 1962 at more than 45 million Chinese – of these, around 7% were tortured and killed by the government, 2% committed suicide and 5% died in Mao’s labour camps built to hold dissidents. [2]




He describes severe punishments for slight infractions, such as being buried alive for stealing a handful of grain or losing an ear and being branded for digging up a potato.










The so-called 

Cultural Revolution

, which began in 1966, was an insanely cruel effort to impose “modernisation” and destroy all that was traditional.




Mao’s Red Guards sought to wipe out the “Four Olds” (old ideas, old culture, old customs, and old habits), often by desecrating historical artifacts and cultural and religious sites. Tens of millions of people were persecuted and sometimes massacred – up to 2 million died. [3]




I have previously explained how the 

Bolshevik

, 

Fascist

 and 

Nazi

 regimes – which likewise combined rabid industrialism with authoritarian terror – were all controlled by the entity I call ZIM, the zio-imperialist mafia. [4] But who could have been behind the nightmarish communist tyranny that subsequently took hold of China?




Yitzhak Shichor of the University of Haifa and Hebrew University of Jerusalem sheds some light on the matter in a fascinating 

paper

 published in the 

International Journal of China Studies

 in 2020.




He writes: “Jews were deeply involved in Communist revolutions in Europe, and primarily in Russia, often in leading positions. This is understandable given their demographic location, extensive education and suffering over the years.




“However, how could we account for the fact that they also played a role in Communist revolutions in Asia, and especially in China? There were practically no Jewish communities to speak of and those few who lived there had been almost totally assimilated, and had no interest whatsoever in Chinese culture, history and politics.




“Still, Jews (who arrived out of China) not only took part in the revolution but had also helped igniting it and then stayed on or joined later”. [5]










Shichor (

pictured

) says of these Jewish participants: “Their main value to the revolution was mainly writing, translation, communication and publication. Although they were all deeply committed to the Chinese Communist revolution, some of them were jailed – for years – and occasionally more than once. Nonetheless, they continued to believe in, and even to justify, the Chinese Communist Party”. [6]




Shichor explains that the Marxist brand of socialism, which reached China via Japan, was initially 

the least attractive

 to Chinese intellectuals.




“Considered too violent, the notions of ‘class struggle’ contradicted traditional Confucian values of harmonious and integrative society, and the thought that ‘workers’ represented the ‘universal’ and ‘revolutionary’ class, did not conform to pre-modern Chinese beliefs…




“Whatever socio-political opposition and ideological radicalism existed, they were articulated not by Marxist communism, but by anarchism. Mao Zedong, one of the founders and later leader of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), regarded himself as anarchist up to the early 1920s”. [7]




But Marxism-Leninism soon came to the fore, thanks to the influence of the Bolsheviks, and Schichor reveals that “many of the chief Soviet and Comintern missionaries in China were Jewish”. [8]




He looks at the signficant role of 

Mikhail Borodin (1884-1951)

, born Mikhail Markovich Gruzenberg, saying that he is usually associated with the Nationalist Party in China (

Guomindang

, GMD), but that “his mission was ultimately and fundamentally to promote the CCP”. [9]










Borodin (

pictured

) was to adopt the usual communist approach of disassociating himself from any particular ethnic roots, but it is interesting to note that at the age of 16 he had joined the 

Bund

 (the General Jewish Workers’ Union), an organisation which placed great emphasis on Jewish identity. [10]




Adolph Abramovich Joffe (1883-1927)

, born in the Crimea to a Jewish-Karaite family and a participant in the Bolshevik revolution, was the Soviet ambassador to the official government in Beijing from 1922 to 1924 and “tried hard to convince Sun Yat-sen [the nationalist revolutionary prime minister] to trust Moscow”. [11]




Shichor writes: “While Marxism-Leninism had existed in parts of China as a 

theory

, turning it into an organized 

activity

 began with Comintern missionaries, headed by 

Grigorii Naumovitch Voitinski [1893-1953]

, who dealt with setting up the CCP… the idea of forming a CCP had already circulated by that time, but no actions had been taken, before his arrival, aged 27, in April 1920″.




Voitinski – born Grigorii Naumovitch Zarkhin to a Jewish family in Nevel, Russia – is considered by historians to have exercised “an immense influence on the Chinese Communist Movement”, he adds. [12]




“In 1920 he became deputy director of the Comintern’s Far Eastern Bureau and left for China, where he met with Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao, the future CCP leaders.




“Although Chen toyed with the Communist idea as early as 1918, he had also been attracted by other ideas (like federalism). It was only after he met Voitinski (

pictured

) that he became committed to Communism, not just in theory but also, and more important, in practice.










“It was following his meetings with Voitinski that the first communist cells had been formed – at least seven in different cities and provinces, before the CCP was organized. Voitinski’s promotion of Marxist study groups not only paved the ground for the establishment of Party cells but also for distributing Marxist-Leninist knowledge that Chinese intellectuals had been lacking”. [13]




“His impact was felt not only in the emergence of anti-US feelings among Chinese intellectuals, but also, and more significantly, in fighting anarchism and in its eventual demise”. [14]




A key role of industrialist and authoritarian communism has always been to crush all real opposition to the empire of greed whose agenda it secretly serves.




As an aside, some insights into Chinese anarchism can be found in an 

essay

 by Robert Scalpino and George T. Yu.




They argue: “Anarchism, whatever its utopian qualities for modern China, was in many respects also naturally Chinese. It was the other side of the Confucian, educative, centralized, authoritarian state. It was the scholar in contemplation and out of office, the peasant out of reach of his landlord, the wanderer beyond the outstretched hands of the state. Indeed, it was the imperishable goal of all men at all times – complete freedom for self realization within the limits of social justice, to the limits of one’s capacity”. [15]










They cite a definition of anarchism that appeared in the movement’s journal 

Hsin Shih chi

 (‘The New Century’) in 1907: “The individual is the basic unit in society. Together with others, he forms a village, and with other villages, a country is formed. Society in turn is formed through the process of bringing all countries together.




“The proper society is that which permits free exchange between and among individuals, mutual aid, the common happiness and enjoyment of all, and the freedom from control by the force of a few. This is what Anarchism seeks to realize.




“The governments of today, however, are organized by the few, who in turn pass laws which are of benefit to the few. Thus the state is the destroyer of the proper society. In sum, what we seek is the destruction of the destroyer of proper society”. [16]




It is quite clear why those out to destroy “proper society” in favour of global “communist” tyranny would want to wipe out the alternative presented by anarchism.




The authors note: “Historically, Marxism was unable to make inroads into China until after the Russian Revolution of 1917 when Lenin’s followers, bankrolled by the Bolshevik government, began their attacks on Anarchists in Russia and neighboring countries…




“There is no better way to see the authoritarian elements in Communist theory than to read the Communist polemics directed against the Anarchist”.










To this effect, they quote the aforementioned Chen (

pictured

), the leading spokesman for the Chinese communists. He described the Chinese people as corrupt and backward and said that, if they were to be saved, there had to be “strict interference” in economic and political matters, an “enlightened despotism”. The chief obstacle to this was the “lazy, wanton, illegal sort of free thought that forms a part of our people’s character”. [17]




Although, from my perspective, many Chinese anarchists at the time were worryingly enthusiastic about “progress” and “science”, Scalpino and Yu add: “Ch’en pursued another theme with vigor: Anarchism would have man return to primitivism. Economically, it would take him back to the era of handicraft industries. Politically, it would remove him to the days of tribalism”. [18]




Chinese revolutionaries were taken to the USSR to undergo Bolshevik brainwashing: in 1925, a first wave of some 340 Chinese students – both GMD and CCP – arrived in Moscow to attend the new Sun Yat-sen University.




The first rector of this institution was 

Karl Radek (1885-1939)

, 

pictured

, who was born Karol Sobelsohn to a Jewish family in Lvov, Ukraine.










Shichor comments: “As the rector of Sun Yat-sen University, he must have influenced Chinese students – both left and right… One of his sentences, published in 1925 and related to the prospects of the CCP to seize power, could be regarded, in retrospect, as a prediction: in the course of its revolutionary struggles, the Chinese proletariat, together with the petty bourgeoisie, ‘will be forced for the time being to develop the economic power of the land in a capitalist fashion'”. [19]




Among the Jewish activists who associated themselves with Chinese communism were a number of Americans, we learn.




One of these was 

Sidney Rittenberg (1921-2019)

: “Influenced by his grandfather (on his mother’s side), who had been a Russian Jewish revolutionary, Rittenberg joined the American Communist Party in 1940 when he was eighteen”. [20]




“When he arrived in China in September 1945, the war was over… Usually, Chinese he met did not know what a Jew was. He began to meet Chinese communists and, as a soldier free to move, did them modest favours – including helping several underground activists to escape from the police”. [21]




“Sometime by late 1946 or early 1947, Rittenberg became a Party member, approved by the top communist leaders, including Mao, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai, Ren Bishi and Zhu De. He was the first US citizen to become a CCP member. His main role was to make information about communist victories – discounted and ignored outside China – available to the West”. [22]










Shichor relates that for a few months in 1967, Rittenberg (

pictured

) was the head of China’s Broadcast Administration (Radio Beijing), at a time “when the Cultural Revolution was turning nasty”.




His activity there apparently led to certain “antisemitic” critics complaining that “Rittenberg shows all the qualities we have long been accustomed to finding in the Jew”. [23]




Shichor relates that after his return to the USA, Rittenberg continued his mission – to “make China more accessible to the West” – but now spurning revolutionary talk for an economic message. [24]




Rittenberg was, it seems, interviewed on CBS network’s 

60 Minutes

 more than any other individual and, in parallel, he founded a consulting firm for American companies doing business in China.




Says Shichor: “He offered his services, personal connections and familiarity with the Chinese system, turning into a full-fledge capitalist, making millions of dollars. As such, he personally embodied the combination post-Mao China has been attempting, a socialist market economy, capitalism under a communist system. This unprecedented innovation was introduced to China mainly by Jewish economists”. [25]




More on that shortly.




Another key Jewish figure in Chinese communism was 

Israel Epstein (1915-2005)

, 

pictured

, whose worldview Shichor describes as “a combination of orthodox Judaism and European enlightened modernism”. [26]










He became a naturalized Chinese citizen and was one of the founders of a pro-industry magazine called 

China Reconstructs

, taking on the role of editor-in-chief in 1979.




Shichor adds: “In 1983, he was admitted to the CPPCC (Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference). Half of its ten non-Chinese members at one time were Jewish. Jews played constructive roles in most of China’s media, directed to the outside world”. [27]




Yet another of these propagandists was 

Sidney Shapiro (1915-2014)

, who was born to a Jewish family in Brooklyn, New York.




“After graduating, he joined a prominent firm of Jewish Wall Street lawyers. He left New York in March 1947, not for any ideological motives or communist inclinations, but hoping to improve his Chinese while seeking a job as a business lawyer for an American firm in Beijing. Through his would-be Chinese wife, he approached the communists…




“Soon employed by the Bureau of Cultural Relations with Foreign Countries, Shapiro became a translator of books and pamphlets. He still insisted that he ‘wasn’t much of a Marxist’”. [28]










“In the early 1960s, Shapiro (

pictured

) finally decided that he had the kind of life he wanted most. He realized he ‘could do more useful and satisfying work in Peking than in New York’, and in 1963 applied for Chinese citizenship, which he received a few months later”. [29]




David Crook (1910-2000)

 was born in London, England, to a Jewish family of Eastern European origins.




He joined the Communist Party in 1936, went off to be part of the International Brigades in the Spanish Civil War and was promptly “recruited by the KGB”. Shichor reveals: “He began spying on leftist ‘elements’ who opposed the Soviet Union, and especially Stalin… In May 1938, on Soviet orders, he left for Shanghai… Officially, he was teaching literature at St. John’s University and later at Suzhou University. Unofficially he spied, especially on ‘Trotskyists'”. [30]




During the Second World War Crook (

pictured below

) joined the RAF and became an officer but was demoted because he was “suspected of spying for the Soviets” – correctly so, presumably! [31]




After the war he went to live in China and by the early 1950s had become deputy dean in the English Department of what was to become the Beijing Foreign Languages Institute.




Shichor explains: “Crook’s teaching concentrated on training interpreters and translators who would escort foreign visitors, rather than ‘wasting’ time on teaching literature he considered ‘impractical’ at best, and ‘intellectual’ at worst. Many of his thousands of students ‘reached the highest ranks in the foreign ministry and in academia'”. [32]










Crook’s propagandistic activities in the 1970s included a three-month-tour in the world outside the communist state “where he spoke in favour of the Cultural Revolution and China”. [33]




A second “British Jew who became full-fledged pro-Chinese spokesman”, as Shichor puts it, was 

Michael Shapiro (1910-1986)

.




I 

see

 that he was actually born in Ukraine, but his family settled in the East End of London and he gained British nationality in 1931. He joined the Young Communist League in 1931 and the Communist Party of Great Britain in 1934. [34]




Shichor says: “In 1949, or 1950, he left for China, reportedly ‘at the invitation of the Chinese Communist Party Central Committee, and on the assignment of the British Communist Party’ and was attached to the China Information Bureau”. [35]




“Michael Shapiro (

pictured

) never returned to the UK. Until his death in 1986, a total of 36 years, he worked at Xinhua News Agency and Foreign Languages Press, copy-editing English commentaries for the Department of Home News for Overseas Service, as well as translating the works of Mao Zedong and Liu Shaoqi. This was the Western ‘foreign experts” – many of them Jewish – main mission, as demonstrated in the following episode.










“In late 1959, the CCP Central Committee decided to form a team to translate a fourth volume of Mao’s 

Selected Works

 into English, and to revise the outdated English translation of the first three volumes, issued by the mid-1950s.




“Work began in early 1960 by a team of fourteen, of which nine were Chinese (Oxford-educated scholars, Foreign Ministry, Foreign Languages Press and Foreign Languages Institute officials) and five foreigners: Sydney Rittenberg, Frank Coe, Israel Epstein, Sol Adler, and Michael Shapiro – all Jewish”. [36]




But Jewish influence on communist China was not merely cultural, as Shichor proudly relates.







In the late 1970s, as soon as Beijing’s post-Mao leaders decided it was time to undertake wide-ranging economic reform (which some had in mind since the early 1950s), discussions were held with leading foreign economic experts, invited to China. Intentionally, or not, most of them were Jewish. Historically, Jews were usually associated with money (capital), for better or for worse. Skilled in commerce and banking, educated, urban yet highly mobile, and with worldwide family connections – Jews represented modernity, and a most significant driving force behind capitalist growth and development. Marx himself specifically equated capitalism with Judaism. Jews also excelled in research: 40 percent of all Nobel Prize winners in economics and 51 percent of all US economics Nobel Prize winners were Jewish. Some of them helped China to become the second – perhaps the leading – world economic power. [37]







The Jewish “experts” invited to red China in 1979 included the economist 

Milton Friedman (1912-2006)

, who accepted and made the trip. [38]




Shichor adds: “Another delegation visited China in 1979. Headed by the University of Pennsylvania Profesor Lawrence Klein (who won the 1980 economics Nobel Prize), it included professor Irma Adelman, [of] the Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics, the Graduate School of the University of California, Berkeley; and Kenneth Arrow of Harvard University (who had won the Nobel Prize in 1972) – all Jewish”. [39]










Then in November 1988 Chinese prime minister Zhao Ziyang met and sought advice from the American-Israeli 

Stanley Fischer (1943-2025)

, who had earlier that year become chief economist of the World Bank. [40]




Fischer 

went on

 to be deputy managing director of the International Monetary Fund, governor of the Bank of Israel and vice chair of the US Federal Reserve. Oh, and he was also an executive at Citigroup, a senior advisor at BlackRock, a “Distinguished Fellow” of the Council on Foreign Relations and a member of the Bilderberg Group. [41]




Are there really still people out there who think that all these global inter-connections are coincidental and that to suggest otherwise is to spread “anti-semitic conspiracy theories”?

author: winter oak
title: Anarchy at the seaside
content:
by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article 

here




One of the more memorable periods in my political activism was with Worthing Anarchist Teapot.




I discovered the other day that evidence of this initiative can still be found on the internet, in archived pages published by the friend who was the main force behind it.




Her aim was to replicate in our English seaside town a project that had been quite a hit down the road in Brighton, namely to set up temporary cafés, offering free tea and coffee, in order to spread the word about anarchism.




The first entry in her 

diary

 is dated October 1 1998 and she records, defiantly eschewing the use of capital letters:* “some brighton anarchist teapot collective members came over and met with us to discuss creating a worthing teapot. lots of interest and ideas to share and we’re well on the way to having our own anarchist teapot now after it being a vague idea that we might act on at some point in the future, it’s now within sight of becoming a reality”.




You can read the full account for yourself if you like (the timeline starts from the bottom of the page) – basically we did manage to open a café in a couple of locations but only very briefly, as things kept going wrong.










An entry on December 19, still in 1998, describes an evening I remember very well indeed: “a couple of collective members spent an hour or two last night doing the rounds of any worthing pub that would let in anarchists! this was the anarchist teapot desperate attempt to raise funds. we managed to raise just over 30 quid from only four pubs (and one of them only had five people in it). so not bad really. and we had an amusing time arguing with pissed-up people. and were told by a middle-aged man: ‘ah, anarchy, that was popular when i was at school'”.




I tried this a decade later, with a different anarchist friend, and it did not work at all. Society (and pubs) had changed a lot in that time.




The New Year saw us adopt a new tactic. “16th january 1999. well, still no premises and no-one to stay overnight, so no prospect of premises for a while either. instead we’ve been taking the teapot to the streets (we did one today and two over christmas/new year). basically this means a wonky trestle table (but with a nice table-cloth!), a tea urn with a very fetching bright red insulating jacket secured with string, fliers, leaflets and zines, a few collective members, and a couple of donations tins. the ‘street teapots’ have been slow, attracting mainly the people who already knew about us. we have reached a fair number of new people though, so not all bad. it’s the suspicious look people give you when you offer them a free cup of tea that’s so disconcerting”.




We then carried out a special “occupation” of a town landmark that we called the “bandstand”, although it was really just some seating under a roof.










“13th february 1999. today the anarchist teapot squatted the bandstand in worthing town centre, declaring it a ‘free tea zone’. brilliant day! really busy and we gave out loads of tea and info to allsorts of people. overall a great response apart from two old ladies who came over tempted by a free cuppa, saw our literature and said ‘we’re not taking tea from anarchists’ before walking off!




“this was so much better than our usual saturday stalls. we had a big black anarchist flag flying, a huge brightly painted banner saying ‘free tea zone’, and lots of balloons. there’re benches in the bandstand so people could sit down and have their tea. all this made an eye-catching and welcoming area. we also had some vegan flapjack and choccy cake – though this didn’t last long! – and we got through two tea urns in about four hours. so … a great success, we’ll definitely be doing this again”.




I don’t think we did, in fact, but the street stalls kept going for a long time, albeit without the friend I have been quoting and, eventually, without the tea, because it was too much work for little purpose (at this point we became simply Worthing Anarchists). My friend Gil and I were the mainstays of this Saturday tradition for a decade and it only stopped when, sadly, he died at the end of 2009.




I also discovered in the internet archives the 

text

 of the little leaflet that we handed out to the good people of Worthing. I know that I basically wrote it, although others in the group may well have made amendments.




Here I have reinserted the capital letters, as I am sure they were there in the printed version!
















Why we are anarchists




For many people in Worthing “anarchist” is probably a word which means very little. If anything, they probably think of violent anti-social trouble-makers, out to create havoc and chaos for no good reason at all.




In fact, the opposite is the truth. The term ‘anarchy’ simply means absence of government and anarchists believe that normal people, left to their own devices, are quite capable of running their own lives and local communities without the self-appointed leaders of Westminster, Brussels or Washington holding the whip hand.




We are currently experiencing a breakdown in natural community life because our self-respect and human values have been eaten away by faceless, money-driven industrial society.




Anarchists want to turn the world’s power structures the other way up. People must come first, not governments and profits.




Although anarchism does admittedly end in ‘-ism’, it is not one of those boring narrow-minded dogmas that most of us would run a mile from.




A love of freedom, truth, justice and nature are the broad planks that bond us together – within that there is plenty of room for diversity.










Anarchists are not the same as the ‘trendy lefties’ you may have come across in the past. For all their politically correct posing, these left-wingers have nothing worthwhile to offer ordinary people.




They still want us all to be slaves to a system – except it would be them and their mates in charge of us, not the current bunch of bastards!




You are going to hear a lot more about anarchism as the new millennium arrives. That is because anarchists are the only people left who have the guts to stand up to the all-powerful global tyranny of finance and business.




The political struggle in the next century isn’t going to be about this party and that party, left and right, tweedledum and tweedledee.




It’s going to be a battle of those who cherish freedom, hope, beauty, health, community and justice against the dark forces of greed, profit, war, technology, starvation and environmental destruction.




As anarchists, we know which side we are on.




Do you?










* This was, after all, just a few short months before the famous Carnival Against Capital in the City of London.
















PS. I have added the “Why we are anarchists” text to the new “

Real Anarchists

” blog.

content:

Ernst Friedrich Schumacher (1911-1977)

 is best remembered for his 1973 book 

Small is Beautiful: A Study of Economics As If People Mattered

 and its message that “infinite growth in a finite environment is an obvious impossibility”. [1]




As the title of the book conveys, he saw it as important to restore a human scale to human self-organisation: “Centralisation is mainly an idea of order; decentralisation, one of freedom”. [2]




Schumacher’s attack on centralisation and economic growth went hand in hand with a broader assault on industrial society itself.




He noted in 

Small is Beautiful

As I explain in my 

profile

ways of thinking

mega-racket

 [5] to gain its stranglehold on our lives.

by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article 

here




The anarchist movement of which I became part in the 1990s was very much to my liking.




It took to the streets against the globalists and their summits, it fiercely defended nature against roadbuilding and other “development” and it was defiantly opposed to the plutocratic ruling class with all its exploitation, repression and warmongering.




Anarchists expressed themselves freely, clearly, angrily and often with a sharp sense of humour.




But, progressively, all of that changed.




Opposing globalist gatherings was deemed retrograde by many, nature was increasingly regarded as a suspect reactionary construct and the emphasis shifted to “critical whiteness” and “trans rights”.




Worst of all, the joy and humour seemed to drain completely away from the movement, being replaced by the dead-eyed and narrow-minded robotic dogmatism which I had always associated with the Marxist “left”.










I began to suspect that the anarchist scene had been deliberately infiltrated and corrupted by the ruling mafia in order to disarm it as a potential source of resistance.




This was confirmed for me six or seven years ago, initially by a general anarchist failure to call out the obvious 

fakery

 of the “climate” movement and then, of course, by the appalling collaboration with the Covid manoeuvre.
